data.text: A complete view of a virtual reality (VR) system consists of the organism, the VR hardware, and the surrounding physical world. Data flow from the organism to the hardware is tracking, while data flow from the hardware to the organism is stimulation, with bidirectional data flows also existing between the hardware, the physical world, and the organism. The organism is an equally important component of the system that cannot be omitted because the user is always present.
points: A VR system consists of the organism, the VR hardware, and the physical world.
Data flows are categorized as tracking from the organism to the hardware and stimulation from the hardware to the organism.
The organism is an equally important component of the system that cannot be omitted.

data.text: Data flow in a VR system is bidirectional: stimulation data carries hardware-generated stimuli that override the user's senses, and tracking data uses sensors to track user motions. Head tracking is commonly used and is the most important thing to track, while tracking may also include button presses, controller movements, eye movements, and movements of other body parts.
points: Data flow between VR hardware and the user is bidirectional.
Head tracking is the most important thing to track, though other motions and button presses may also be tracked.

data.text: The virtual reality system consists of the user, the hardware, and the surrounding physical environment. The environment is included because it may affect user behavior through real-world stimuli. Additionally, the physical environment can be changed by the user's movements or by the hardware, which may track, change, or deal with objects.
points: The virtual reality system consists of the user, the hardware, and the surrounding physical environment.
The physical environment is part of the VR system because it may affect user behavior through real-world stimuli.
A user's physical movement may change the surrounding physical environment.
VR hardware may track, change, or deal with objects in the physical environment.

data.text: Virtual reality (VR) hardware has three major components: displays, sensors, and computers. Displays are output devices that stimulate the user's sensory organs, while sensors are input devices that track user movements and real-world information. Computers act as processing devices that process inputs and produce outputs for the user to perceive the world.
points: VR hardware has three major components: displays, sensors, and computers.
Displays are output devices that stimulate the user's sensory organs.
Sensors are input devices that track user movements and extract information from the real world.
Computers are processing devices that process inputs and produce outputs.

data.text: VR hand input devices fall into five broad categories: world-grounded, non-tracked handheld, tracked handheld, hand-worn, and bare-hand. While world-grounded and non-tracked handheld devices have limitations regarding portability and presence, tracked handheld controllers provide 3D tracking but may limit physical interaction. Hand-worn devices like data gloves offer natural interaction but can require frequent recalibration, while bare-hand inputs like Leap Motion leave the user's hands completely free but may cause fatigue or require line-of-sight.
points: VR hand input devices fall into five broad categories: world-grounded, non-tracked handheld, tracked handheld, hand-worn, and bare-hand.
World-grounded devices like joysticks have portability issues, while non-tracked handheld controllers may cause break-in presence.
Tracked handheld controllers, such as VIVE controllers, provide 3D tracking but may limit the ability to feel passive virtual objects.
Hand-worn devices like data gloves provide natural interaction but can require frequent recalibration and may cause discomfort.
Bare-hand inputs like Leap Motion leave the user's hands completely free but may require line-of-sight and can cause fatigue.

data.text: Non-hand-based input devices capture input from body parts other than the hands, such as head motion and eye gaze. Head-tracking and eye tracking allow a system to change the view and infer actions, but eye tracking can suffer from the Midas touch problem where actions are performed from habitual gazes. Consequently, multimodal input is generally preferred over eye tracking alone to avoid actions performed from unintentional gazes.
points: Non-hand-based input devices capture input from body parts other than the hands.
Head-tracking devices use head motion to change the view.
Eye tracking devices track eye movements to help the system infer actions.
The Midas touch problem is the inability to distinguish intentional gazes from habitual gazes.
Multimodal input is generally preferred over eye tracking alone to avoid unintentional actions.

data.text: VR hardware must be understood from the overall system point of view, considering the multiple components of the system and how they interact with the hardware. The three major hardware components of any virtual reality system are input, output, and processor.
points: VR hardware must be understood from an overall system point of view.
The three major hardware components are input, output, and processor.
